A complementary, data-driven analysis correlates temperature and ‐ residence time to property evolution, identifying temperature as the dominant degradative factor and providing predictive models (e.g., response surfaces, SVMs/ANNs) for setting operating conditions that minimize property loss. The practical implication is that process control—not just materials screening—can recover value from recycled PP by dialing temperatures, screw speeds, and residence times to the “safe zone” predicted by the model. The mechanical studies make a compelling contrast with the STRAP results: where multiple melt histories promote chain scission and broadened molecular-weight distributions, dissolution-based recovery preserves molecular structure and removes additives/pigments, yielding near-virgin rheology and optical performance. For converters, this can be the difference between down-cycling into thick, less demanding parts versus maintaining film-grade performance where process stability and drawability hinge on extensional viscosity. Topic Area 3 – Thermal Depolymerization of Mixed Plastic Waste Streams Understanding how processing conditions influence pyrolysis product yields and composition is essential for designing efficient chemical recycling systems. Because different reactors and operating parameters can significantly alter the distribution of oils, waxes, and gases, comparative studies help identify the conditions that maximize desirable products and improve overall process viability. Virgin and post-consumer (PC) waste plastics were pyrolyzed using lab-scale fluidized-bed reactors at Iowa State University (0.5 kg/hr) and the University of Wisconsin-Madison (0.12 kg/hr) at different pyrolysis temperatures (600 °C vs 500 °C) and vapor retention times (1s vs 20s). The condensable yields were lower in the reactor with a longer vapor residence time. For example, pyrolysis of PC high-density polyethylene (HDPE) yielded 79% of condensable (the sum of wax and oil) from Iowa State University’s reactor and 69.8% from the University of Wisconsin-Madison’s reactor. In addition to the yields, there were significant variations in the compositions of the condensables. The higher reactor temperature and short residence time produced primarily wax (73% of C20+ hydrocarbons), whereas the lower reactor temperature and longer vapor residence time produced mostly light oils (e.g., 49.3% of hydrocarbons with boiling points <175 °C). Pyrolysis and thermo-oxo degradation (TOD) were compared using a lab-scale fluidized reactor at Iowa State University. TOD uses air with a controlled oxygen concentration (2- 8 vol%) as the environment gas to decompose plastics. Due to exothermic oxidation, TOD could substantially reduce energy demand for decomposing plastics. TOD produced much more gases than pyrolysis due to increased CO production (e.g., 19% CO with 2 2 4% O vs 9% CO with 0% O for PC-HDPE). However, the condensable yields from the 2 2 2 two methods were comparable (e.g., 75% vs. 79%). In addition to hydrocarbon waxes and oils, TOD also produced a small fraction of aqueous oils containing acids, alcohols, and ketones. The effects of plastic pre-washing were investigated by comparing the conversion of virgin plastics and unwashed PC waste plastics.
